tldr: We propose LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model that projects tactile sensors with different physical principles into a unified space and pre-trains on 5,000 hours of data using latent space prediction (Tactile-JEPA), dramatically boosting robot dexterous manipulation across sensor discrepancies and unseen hardware.
hero_caption: An overview of LingBot-Touch. The top row shows heterogeneous data based on different physical principles—piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile—integrated into a shared fingertip geometric space. The bottom row shows how the pre-trained encoder can be kept frozen and seamlessly applied to contact physical property estimation, imitation learning (VLA), and reinforcement learning policies.
overview:
Humans can move their fingertips dexterously even with their eyes closed because of the sense of touch. However, dexterous manipulation in robotics still relies heavily on vision, struggling to capture occluded contacts, minute slips, and pressing forces. The biggest reason lies in the differing physical principles of tactile sensors. Piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors (which image gel deformation via cameras) differ completely in channel counts, spatial resolutions, and sampling rates, making it extremely difficult to train a single model on combined data.

To tackle this, the authors built a common interface that strips away sensor-specific physics by geometrically mapping any tactile signal onto a Canonical Spherical Space. They then constructed an unprecedented tactile dataset totaling roughly 5,000 hours (over 460,000 episodes) collected from human tactile gloves and bimanual robot teleoperation. On this massive corpus, they trained LingBot-Touch, a unified tactile foundation model, using Tactile-JEPA—an extension of the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), well known in self-supervised image and video learning, tailored for touch.

During evaluation, the pre-trained encoder weights were kept completely frozen. In physical probing tasks estimating contact force and location, the model demonstrated remarkable zero-shot generalization even to an unseen magnetic sensor hand (XHand1) never encountered during pre-training. Furthermore, across 26 bimanual real-robot tasks, adding this model's tactile tokens into state-of-the-art policies like Diffusion Policy, $\pi_{0.5}$, and LingBot-VLA improved success rates by an average of 14 to 26 percentage points. Feeding raw tactile signals only improved success rates by about half as much and even degraded performance in some cases, proving that having an appropriately abstracted contact representation—rather than merely having touch data—is the key to unlocking robot dexterity.
contributions: Constructed a massive, multi-source tactile dataset spanning roughly 5,000 hours and 1.33 billion frames, covering the three major sensor types: piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile.

Established a tactile foundation model capable of zero-shot adaptation to unseen sensors without fine-tuning, enabled by a Canonical Spherical Space that normalizes sensor-specific layouts, 5D RoPE, and Tactile-JEPA based on latent space prediction.

Demonstrated that simply plugging in frozen tokens significantly improves dexterous manipulation performance across 26 real-robot tasks (4 imitation and VLA policies) and 12 simulation tasks (reinforcement learning).
Demonstrated that scaling pre-training data volume (1K to 5K hours) and model capacity monotonically improves contact understanding and robot manipulation performance.

sections.heading: Why Have Robots Struggled to Utilize the Sense of Touch?
sections.summary: Although commercial tactile sensors exist, their differing physical principles and signal formats have prevented pooling large datasets to build foundation models like those in vision and NLP. LingBot-Touch breaks through this barrier, unifying data from heterogeneous sensors to learn general contact representations with a single encoder.
sections.details:
When a person's fingertips are numbed, even lighting a match or buttoning a shirt becomes difficult despite having intact vision. That is how indispensable touch is for dexterous manipulation. Yet, most modern robot learning models rely entirely on vision. Vision alone cannot accurately detect what happens behind the fingers, how much force is applied, or whether an object is slipping.

Touch has failed to scale not because sensors do not exist, but due to three key absences:
- No common input format (resolutions, channels, and layouts vary drastically across sensors)
- No large-scale corpus (data is fragmented by sensor type and cannot be pooled)
- No established learning recipe (studies remained confined to isolated sensors and tasks)

However, consider this: the physical contact event of a fingertip pressing against an edge is fundamentally the same phenomenon, whether measured by a magnetic sensor, electrical resistance changes, or a camera capturing gel deformation. In other words, if sensor-specific physics can be properly abstracted away, a shared contact representation can be learned.

Based on this insight, this work introduces LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model. By arranging tactile elements (taxels) on a shared fingertip spherical surface and training via latent space prediction (Tactile-JEPA), it achieves surprising adaptability, generalizing to unseen sensors without any fine-tuning.

sections.heading: Evolution of Tactile Sensing and Self-Supervised Learning
sections.summary: We review diverse tactile sensing technologies (magnetic, optical, and resistive) alongside the lineage of self-supervised representation learning (especially JEPA methods) that rapidly advanced in vision and video. We position how this method overcomes the sensor dependency and modality fragmentation of prior tactile models.
sections.details:
### Diversity of Tactile Sensing
Robotic tactile sensors employ various physical principles. Magnetic sensors such as ReSkin, AnySkin, and PaXini capture magnetic field variations. Visuotactile sensors like GelSight, DIGIT, and Sharpa Wave use miniature cameras to capture gel deformation. Meanwhile, piezoresistive and capacitive sensors such as STAG and DexSkin utilize changes in electrical resistance or capacitance. While measuring the same contacts, their spatial resolutions, sampling frequencies, and channel semantics differ entirely.

### Self-Supervised Representation Learning and Tactile Applications
Recent progress in foundation models has been driven by contrastive learning and self-distillation (e.g., DINO), masked reconstruction (e.g., MAE), and Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (e.g., I-JEPA and V-JEPA).
In robotics, tactile models such as Sparsh, AnyTouch, T3, and FTP-1 have been proposed, but they remained restricted to specific optical sensors or required per-sensor adapters to handle heterogeneous hardware, falling short of full unification. LingBot-Touch addresses these challenges at once through a multi-branch tokenizer and a shared Haptic Transformer.

sections.heading: LingBot-Touch Architecture and Training Mechanism
sections.summary: By collecting a 5,000-hour multi-source tactile corpus, mapping taxels to a Canonical Spherical Space with 5D RoPE, and applying Tactile-JEPA with a mask warm-up for sparse signals, the model learns sensor-agnostic contact representations.
sections.details:
### 3.1 5,000-Hour Tactile Corpus
The major bottleneck in tactile data collection is the operational cost on physical robots. In this work, human-worn piezoresistive gloves (~2,197 hours) and magnetic gloves (~1,136 hours) were utilized to efficiently gather daily manipulation data. Combined with bimanual robot teleoperation data using Sharpa Wave visuotactile hands (~1,650 hours), the dataset reached an unprecedented scale of 4,983 hours, 464K episodes, and 1.33 billion frames. Tasks span 24 categories including tool use, opening/closing, and assembly.

### 3.2 Tactile-JEPA and Canonical Spherical Space
To align taxel layouts that vary across sensors, a Canonical Spherical Space was defined by mapping each fingertip to a reference sphere of unit radius. Each taxel receives a 5D address $a_i = (t_i, f_i, p_i) \in \mathbb{R}^5$ consisting of a time window, finger index, and 3D coordinate, which is fed into the shared Haptic Transformer (HaT) via 5D Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE).

For pre-training, Tactile-JEPA predicts latent features rather than reconstructing raw signals. Since tactile signals are predominantly zero-valued when no contact occurs (highly sparse), reconstructing raw pixels or signals leads the model to focus on reproducing empty backgrounds. Predicting masked features in latent space forces the model to extract the essential physical structure of contact.
Additionally, to prevent training instabilities early on, a mask warm-up strategy is introduced, starting the spatial mask ratio at 40% and linearly ramping it up to 80% over the first 300 steps.

### 3.3 Layout-Agnostic Data Augmentations
To prevent the model from overfitting to specific sensor taxel patterns, multi-resolution sampling dynamically resamples spatial resolution, and position perturbation injects small random shifts to taxel coordinates within neighborhood bounds. This grants strong generalization to unseen sensors.

Signals from heterogeneous sensors are mapped onto the canonical spherical space, processed by shallow tokenizers, fed into a shared Transformer with 5D RoPE, and trained by predicting masked features in latent space.

sections.heading: How Well Does It Capture Physical Contact Properties?
sections.summary: We evaluated physical property estimation from the frozen encoder using linear probing. The model demonstrated superior accuracy on pre-trained sensors and an unseen magnetic sensor, with performance scaling monotonically as dataset size and model capacity increased.
sections.details:
### 4.1-4.2 Contact Physics Probing with Frozen Encoders
Keeping encoder weights completely frozen and attaching lightweight probe heads, five probing tasks were evaluated: Force Recovery, Contact Center, Contact Area, Future Force, and Tactile to Video Retrieval.

- **Results on Known Sensor (Sharpa Wave)**: Compared to the prior tactile foundation model FTP-1 (which uses sensor-specific adapters), LingBot-Touch significantly reduced force error from 2.31 N to 0.81 N and contact center error by an order of magnitude from 2.19 mm to 0.12 mm. Video retrieval Top-5 recall jumped dramatically from 16.5% to 72.6%.
- **Zero-Shot Results on Unseen Sensor (XHand1)**: When directly applied without adapters to the magnetic hand XHand1 (entirely absent from pre-training), LingBot-Touch achieved a contact center error of 0.16 mm (versus 5.89 mm for FTP-1 with its dedicated adapter) and a force error of 1.32 N (versus 3.72 N for FTP-1).

### 4.3 Scaling Laws and Cross-Sensor Synergy
Scaling data from 1,000 to 5,000 hours yielded monotonic performance gains across all tasks for the Small model. Crucially, cross-sensor data sharing proved effective: even when magnetic sensor data was limited, co-pre-training with piezoresistive and optical data substantially improved contact force and dynamics estimation on the magnetic sensor. Contact intensity and temporal dynamics transfer across physical sensing principles.

### 4.4 Latent Prediction (JEPA) vs. Signal Reconstruction (VAE/MAE)
Comparing against VAE and MAE which reconstruct in signal space, VAE suffered performance degradation as data scaled because learning was dominated by uncontacted background areas. In contrast, LingBot-Touch's latent predictive approach scaled smoothly with data volume, decisively outperforming MAE.

### 4.6 Latent Space Visualization
UMAP feature visualizations revealed that non-contact states cluster into a single region, while the progression from initial contact to pressing, unloading, and detachment unfolds along a smooth, continuous trajectory.

sections.heading: Integration into Robot Policies and Substantial Gains
sections.summary: We tested on 26 real bimanual manipulation tasks and 12 simulated dexterous tasks. Simply attaching frozen LingBot-Touch tokens produced large improvements in policy success rates, highlighting a critical gap compared to feeding raw signals.
sections.details:
### 5.1-5.2 Real Bimanual Robot Evaluation Across 26 Tasks
Using Sharpa Wave (20 tasks) and XHand1 (6 tasks), 26 touch-critical tasks were conducted, including page turning, SD card insertion/removal, spray trigger squeezing, egg transfer, and hardness sorting. Four policy backbones were tested: Diffusion Policy, $\pi_{0.5}$, LingBot-VLA, and T-Rex, with a tiny frozen encoder of just 5.46M parameters added (increasing policy parameter count by under 0.2%).

- **Substantial Success Rate Improvements**: Average success rates across 26 tasks jumped from 21.6% to 35.6% (+14.0 pt) for Diffusion Policy, from 48.1% to 69.9% (+21.8 pt) for $\pi_{0.5}$, from 48.3% to 73.1% (+24.8 pt) for LingBot-VLA, and from 45.4% to 68.6% (+23.2 pt) for T-Rex.
- **Why Raw Signals Fall Short**: Feeding raw tactile signals directly into policies only provided modest gains of 6 to 11 pt on average, and degraded performance below baseline on delicate tasks like egg transfer and mahjong tile identification. Interpreting high-dimensional, sparse raw touch data from ~200 demonstration episodes from scratch is difficult, underscoring the importance of high-quality pre-trained representations.
- **Dramatic Impact on Unseen Hardware**: On XHand1, adding raw signals provided virtually no benefit (-1.7 pt for $\pi_{0.5}$), whereas adding LingBot-Touch tokens delivered a dramatic +24.5 pt improvement.

### 5.3 Simulation Reinforcement Learning (12 Tasks)
In challenging tasks like pen spinning, ball balancing, and blind grasping trained with PPO, policies utilizing LingBot-Touch features reached an average success rate of 69.0%, outperforming task-specific CNN features (45.6%), raw signals (38.5%), and touch-free baselines (21.4%). Furthermore, cross-seed variance was minimal, stabilizing exploration.

### 5.4 Direct Link Between Pre-Training Scale and Policy Performance
As pre-training data expanded from 1K to 5K hours, LingBot-VLA's average success rate climbed monotonically from 69.8% to 82.2%, confirming that representation quality directly translates to physical task performance.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: LingBot-Touch establishes the viability of a tactile foundation model that unifies heterogeneous sensors and transfers to unseen hardware. By demonstrating tactile scaling laws, this work solidifies the standard role of touch in embodied AI.
sections.details:
This paper presented LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model uniting piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile modalities. With a canonical spherical space providing a unified input format and Tactile-JEPA tailored for sparse signals, the model demonstrates high-quality contact representations across diverse hardware, including unseen sensors.

The most important takeaway is that robots do not require thousands of hours collected on a single sensor: data easily collected from human-worn gloves significantly enhances manipulation intelligence on different robot hands. This shifts tactile data scaling strategies fundamentally.

Currently noted limitations include:
- Validating across a broader range of hand morphologies
- Incorporating capacitive sensors, which were omitted due to data quality hurdles
- Expanding the geometric formulation from fingertips to whole-hand surfaces such as palms

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details and Simulation Setup
sections.summary: Detailed specifications of the pre-training corpus, probing hyper-parameters, real-robot task scoring criteria, and simulated tactile generation and RL setups are covered.
sections.details:
### Dataset and Probing Details
The pre-training corpus incorporates Juqiao (9 taxels/finger, 100 Hz), Xspark (16 taxels, 60 Hz), and TACHIN (61-124 taxels, 60 Hz) piezoresistive gloves; PaXini (96-116 taxels, 41.7-83.3 Hz) magnetic gloves; and Sharpa Wave (240x240 downsampled to 96 points, 30 Hz) visuotactile hands.
For probing, multi-layer features (4 layers) from the encoder are concatenated into a lightweight head with cross-attention pooling and linear layers, trained with AdamW (learning rate $10^{-4}$) for 100 epochs.

### Simulated Tactile Generation and Evaluation
In simulation RL, following TacMap, geometric penetration depth is computed via GPU raycasting against the fingertip surface mesh to generate deformation maps as tactile signals.
In simulated physical probing, pre-trained LingBot-Touch achieved a high Dice score (0.708) in identifying contact regions, confirming that representations learned on real-world data transfer smoothly into simulation.

takeaways: Even when tactile sensors rely on different physical mechanisms, the physical contact event is shared, enabling joint learning under a single encoder via canonical spherical mapping and latent predictive modeling (JEPA).
Using easily collectible human tactile glove data for large-scale pre-training substantially elevates contact understanding and control performance on target robot hands.

Feeding raw touch signals directly into robot policies (VLA or Diffusion Policy) leads to brittle learning; providing abstracted tokens from a pre-trained model is essential for boosting task success rates.
limitations: The current geometric mapping is limited to fingertips, leaving extension to the entire hand surface—such as palms and finger bases—for future work.
Capacitive sensors were excluded from the pre-training corpus due to data quality criteria.
Real-robot evaluations were conducted on two hand types (Sharpa Wave and XHand1), warranting further verification across more diverse hand mechanisms.
